analysis.title: The AI Buildout Is Becoming a Long Credit Issue
key_insights: Hyperscalers are financing a large share of their AI capex in the corporate bond market. Hundreds of billions of dollars have been issued and more is expected, so credit benchmarks are concentrating in companies tied to the AI buildout.

Bondholders get coupons and principal and little of the upside if a company beats expectations. They share in the downside through higher leverage, rating downgrades, wider spreads and default risk. Equity holders take both sides, so the right question for bond investors is whether every participant earns adequate returns on invested capital, not whether AI succeeds.

Corporate bond benchmarks weight issuers by debt outstanding, while equity benchmarks weight by market value. Bond indices therefore add exposure to the largest borrowers whether or not they earn good returns.

The seven leading AI hyperscalers (ORCL, AMZN, META, MSFT, GOOGL, NVDA, SPCX) are among the largest issuers in the Bloomberg U.S. Long Credit Index. Their combined weight rose from 4.1% to 7.5% between September 2025 and September 2026, and the authors say it could more than double over the next two years if issuance proceeds as expected.

The same seven issuers rose from 1.5% to 3.8% of the Bloomberg U.S. Intermediate Credit Index over the same period. The concentration is therefore larger in long credit, where LDI investors buying the longest-dated bonds take on the most incremental exposure.

There is a potential mismatch between the decades-long maturity of the bonds and the shorter horizon over which the technology and its economics will be tested. Computing hardware can become obsolete quickly, and the revenue models, utilization rates and returns on data center spending are uncertain. The authors note that corporate balance sheets, not individual assets, support the bonds.

Past debt-financed buildouts also concentrated benchmarks in a few issuers: financials before the GFC, shale-era energy producers, late-1990s telecom and internet infrastructure, and 19th-century U.S. railroads. In each case the underlying growth story was real, but fixed income returns diverged from economic growth. The authors say they are not claiming AI will follow the same path.

Allspring pitches its U.S. Small Issuer Long Credit (SILC) strategy as a complement to conventional long credit mandates in a multi-manager structure. It covers the smaller 90% of long credit issuers, which reduces dependence on the largest benchmark borrowers, and Allspring says it was designed for broader structural issues rather than as an AI call.

Conclusion: avoiding the eventual losers may matter as much as picking winners, and a more diversified approach may improve LDI portfolio efficiency. Investors should check whether their credit portfolios hold more of a speculative, debt-financed growth theme than intended.

sector_views.rationale: The report does not issue a formal rating. It argues that issuance-weighted benchmarks give long credit investors growing, asymmetric exposure to a debt-financed speculative growth theme.

trade_ideas.description: Add Allspring U.S. Small Issuer Long Credit (SILC) alongside conventional benchmark-oriented long credit managers in a multi-manager structure
trade_ideas.rationale: It focuses on the smaller 90% of long credit issuers, which reduces exposure to issuance-driven thematic concentrations and adds issuer and alpha diversification.

risk_factors: Hyperscaler issuer concentration in long credit benchmarks could more than double within two years.
Duration mismatch between decades-long bonds and a technology and monetization horizon that will be tested sooner.
Computing hardware can become economically obsolete quickly, and returns and utilization on data center spending are uncertain.
Not every participant in the AI race will earn adequate returns on invested capital, which could lead to higher leverage, downgrades and spread widening.
Bondholders have limited upside if the AI cycle exceeds expectations.
vol_and_positioning: Hyperscaler share of the Bloomberg U.S. Long Credit Index rose from 4.1% to 7.5% between September 2025 and September 2026. Share of the Intermediate Credit Index rose from 1.5% to 3.8%.

tension_points.bull_case: The secular AI growth story may prove highly successful, and leading hyperscalers may earn returns that justify the capex. The report notes that the issuers' balance sheets, not individual assets, support the bonds.
tension_points.bear_case: Bondholders get coupons and principal but little upside if AI exceeds expectations. They share in the downside if a debt-financed participant earns inadequate returns, through leverage, downgrades and spread widening. Long-dated bonds may outlast the useful life of the computing hardware.

theme_stances.key_argument: Issuance-weighted bond benchmarks concentrate long credit portfolios in debt-financed AI spenders while bondholders lack the equity upside.
theme_stances.evidence: Bond investors participate much more in the downside than the upside.
